column2: Use the valuation tool that suits each kind of company.
An established company with steady profit: the same E/P and “how many years until I get my money back” is enough.
A company with a big project on the way, or whose profit is changing: you need to count future years’ money separately (DCF).
Holding: the value of its assets (NAV). Banks and insurers: with caution, using book value and lasting profit.
For the price of a finished flat, you look at its rent; for land where a building is going to go up, you have to work out what it will be worth once built.
Each company, its own tool
Free cash flow means the money that’s really left over after all the costs and necessary investment.
You bring future years’ money back to today’s value and add it up; you subtract debt to leave the value of the shares.
In Iran, count the cost of replacing machines at today’s prices, not the old book price; and dollar debt at today’s dollar.
The money left in your account each month after rent, loan payments, household costs and car repairs is your free cash flow.
Money that’s really left over
In textbooks, the return needed on shares is worked out with a formula called CAPM and a number called “beta”.
On the Tehran exchange beta isn’t reliable; queues, price limits and ticker halts separate the daily price from value.
A simpler, more honest way is to build the rate piece by piece.
Instead of guessing how risky a house is with a complicated formula, you ask piece by piece: the area, its age, the deed, the neighbours.
Start from the risk-free return: the return on 2 to 3-year government bonds (Akhza).
Add a few percent for stock risk, usually 5 to 10 points, the same for every company.
Add 0 to 10 more points for each company’s own risk: thin trading, dependence on government decisions, heavy dollar debt, weak management.
Work out the company’s cost of borrowing from finance costs divided by loans.
Like working out a lorry’s fare: the base fare, plus extra for a dirt road, plus extra for fragile goods.
Build the discount rate piece by piece
The most common mistake is to work out inflated numbers with a rate without inflation, or the other way round.
Either do everything with inflated prices and an inflated rate, or everything with today’s prices and a real rate.
To start, the today’s-prices way is simpler: a rate of 38% with 30% inflation means a real rate of about 6.2%.
In this method, don’t forget the cost of replacing machines and the money inflation swallows in receivables and inventory.
If you count your salary in this year’s tomans, you must count your costs in this year’s tomans too; not one this year and one five years from now.
After a few years of forecasts, the rest of the company’s life is summed up in one number: the “terminal value”.
Usually 70 to 85% of the total value comes from this one number; so be very careful with it.
Don’t take long-term real growth above 2%, and always write down what percentage of the value came from this number.
When you price an orchard, the first few years’ fruit is only a small part; most of the value comes from the long years after, which are harder to guess.
“Company C” is a made-up example. With this card’s assumptions, each share is worth about 3,049 rials.
About 75% of this value came from the “terminal value”.
If the discount rate changes by just 1 point, the value moves 15 to 25%. So write a range instead of one number.
If someone asks what your house is worth, the most honest answer is “between 4 and 5 billion”, not “4 billion 312 million”.
In Iran the main driver of value is usually the dollar rate, raw-material prices or government-set prices, not the details of the discount rate.
So build three cases: bad, normal and good, and give each a probability.
The weighted average is about 3,006 rials; but more important is that the value lies between 2,015 and 3,912.
Like a travel plan: if the weather is good, normal, or it snows; you have a separate plan and budget for each.
Another method: compare the company with similar companies.
Find 4 to 6 companies in the same group, compare normal profits for the same period, take the middle number (median) and explain the differences.
Be careful: a past P/E with one-off profit misleads, and P/B in Iran has old book numbers.
For a flat’s price, you ask the prices of 5 similar flats in the same street and compare by size and floor.
Put the three methods side by side to see the value range.
The market price is 2,200; so the market has roughly priced in the bad case.
This is a “margin of safety”, not an instruction to buy: you still need to check the warning bells, profit quality and the comparison with Akhza.
If a car worth between 450 and 700 million is sold for 490, its price is near the lowest value; it’s a good opportunity, but you still need to have it inspected.
A ready-made Excel file that links the three financial statements for the next five years and works out the value per share. Its example is a made-up company.
Sheets: guide, historical (fill from Codal), assumptions, model, and valuation.
Colours: blue means your input, black a formula, green a link from another sheet. Only change the blue ones.
Like a ready-made loan calculator: you just enter the amount and rate, and it works out the rest.
Net profit is added to shareholders’ equity and dividends are taken out of it.
If money owed by customers and inventory grow, cash goes down.
Fixed assets = last year + new purchases − wear and tear.
At the end, assets must equal debts plus shareholders’ equity; if they don’t, there’s a mistake somewhere.
Like the monthly household accounts: start-of-month balance + income − spending = end-of-month balance. If it doesn’t match the bank account, you wrote something down wrong.
The risk is one-sided: in the bad case, if each year the selling price rises just 1% less than inflation and raw materials 1% more, the value falls 54%.
Inflation makes profit look bigger on paper, but the real cost of replacing machines takes it back.
Real cash is less than profit because inflation makes receivables and inventory bigger. And from year three the tax exemption ends.
If two valuation methods are far apart, find the reason; taking the average isn’t the answer.
If two experts give very different prices for a house, you don’t take the average; you ask what one saw that the other didn’t.
Enter two years of a real company’s audited financial statements on the “historical” sheet.
If the latest report covers only some months, build the last 12 months’ profit: last year + this year’s months − the same months last year.
Enter dollar debt at today’s dollar and today’s Akhza return, run the three cases and note the result with the date.
This model is for a single-product company; judge a holding by the value of its assets.
For income over the last 12 months to the end of Khordad: last year’s total income + this year’s first three months − last year’s first three months.
